messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
To find how far a car travels horizontally in a given time \(t\) when launched with an initial speed \(v\) at an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal, you can use the basic projectile motion equations.

### Horizontal Distance Traveled in Time \(t\)

The horizontal component of the velocity is:
\[
v_x = v \cos(\theta)
\]

Since horizontal acceleration is zero (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal distance \(x(t)\) after time \(t\) is simply:
\[
x(t) = v_x \, t = v \cos(\theta) \, t
\]

So the car will travel a horizontal distance of \(v \cos(\theta) \, t\).

---

### Total Range Until Landing

If you’re interested in the total horizontal distance the car will cover before it lands (i.e., the range), you can use:
\[
R = \frac{v^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}
\]
where \(g \approx 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2\) is the acceleration due to gravity.

---

#### Example Calculation

Suppose you have:
- Initial velocity \(v = 20\,\text{m/s}\)
- Launch angle \(\theta = 30^\circ\)
- Time \(t = 3\,\text{s}\)

First, convert the angle to radians if needed (though cosine works directly with degrees in many calculators):
\[
\theta_{\text{rad}} = 30^\circ \times \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.5236\,\text{rad}
\]

Compute the horizontal distance:
\[
x(3) = 20 \cos(30^\circ) \times 3 \approx 20 \times 0.8660 \times 3 \approx 51.96\,\text{m}
\]

So the car would travel approximately **52 m** horizontally in 3 seconds.

---

If you’d like to plug in specific numbers or need help with a particular scenario, just let me know the values of \(v\), \(\theta\), and \(t\)!
